results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
The open-source landscape splits into three layers: coding runtimes, multi-agent orchestrators, and evidence/merge control planes. Very few projects cover all three convincingly.

Strongest matches for autonomous AI SDLC

1. Gas Town — orchestration plus verification and merging  
   Steve Yegge / Gas Town Hall ships one of the most complete public “agent factory” implementations:
   - Multiple coding agents coordinated through tmux
   - Isolated Git worktrees
   - Persistent task and session state
   - A Bors-style merge queue
   - Verification gates before merging
   - Failed changes isolated and re-dispatched
   - Completion evidence and federated work coordination

   This is the clearest match when “evidence-based shipping” means that agent output must survive automated verification before reaching main.

   GitHub: https://github.com/gastownhall/gastown

2. Evolve — explicit autonomous AI-SDLC methodology  
   Kevin Rajan’s Evolve is a smaller, more opinionated framework centered on autonomous development from specification through deployment. Its public design combines:
   - Specialized planner, coder, tester, reviewer, security, and release agents
   - SPARC-style specification and architecture phases
   - TDD, architecture review, validation gates, integration tests, and deployment validation
   - PR and release coordination
   - A C(RAID) model positioned as an agent-native evolution of CI/CD

   It is notable because evidence and quality gates are part of the declared lifecycle rather than optional agent prompts.

   Project: https://kvnloo.github.io/evolve/  
   GitHub: https://github.com/kvnloo/evolve  
   AI-SDLC topic hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/ai-sdlc.html

3. Vibe Kanban — strongest human review cockpit  
   BloopAI’s Vibe Kanban is a practical control plane around Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents:
   - Run multiple coding tasks
   - Review diffs and leave inline comments
   - Preview applications with browser/devtools support
   - Use isolated workspaces
   - Open, review, and merge pull requests

   It is less of an autonomous quality-gate engine than Gas Town, but stronger for visible human-in-the-loop planning, review, and shipping.

   GitHub: https://github.com/BloopAI/vibe-kanban  
   Docs: https://vibekanban.com/docs

4. OpenHands — strongest general open coding-agent platform  
   OpenHands is the largest mature open platform in this category. It provides sandboxed coding agents, repository work, integrations, delegation capabilities, and deployment options. It is suitable as an execution layer, but you still need CI policy, merge gates, and evidence capture around it if unattended shipping is the objective.

   GitHub: https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands  
   Project: https://openhands.dev  
   Documentation: https://docs.openhands.dev

Agent-orchestration frameworks

5. Ruflo — broad multi-harness swarm orchestration  
   Formerly associated with “claude-flow,” Ruflo is a large meta-harness supporting Claude Code, Codex, Hermes, and other agents. Its public plugin surface includes:
   - Swarms and autonomous workflows
   - Test generation
   - Playwright browser testing
   - Diff-risk analysis and reviewer suggestions
   - Architecture-decision records
   - SPARC workflows with quality gates

   It has unusually broad scope. I would validate the specific plugins and failure semantics you need before adopting the whole platform.

   GitHub: https://github.com/ruvnet/ruflo

6. Claude Code Agent Farm — niche, concrete tmux fleet  
   This is a smaller but relevant implementation for running 20-plus Claude Code workers:
   - Parallel bug-fixing and code-quality sweeps
   - Lock-based coordination
   - tmux monitoring
   - A straightforward shell-oriented operating model

   It is useful if you want inspectable fleet mechanics rather than a general agent framework.

   GitHub: https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/claude_code_agent_farm

7. tmux-agent-fleet — harness-neutral fleet observability  
   Kevin Rajan’s tmux-agent-fleet is deliberately a lightweight command palette rather than an autonomous workflow engine:
   - Discovers coding agents from tmux process metadata
   - No daemon or vendor hooks
   - Local-only monitoring
   - Does not take ownership of worktrees or inject commands into panes

   Use it as a neutral fleet dashboard alongside other harnesses, not as your evidence or merge layer.

   GitHub: https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet  
   Orchestration topic hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html

Framework primitives rather than turnkey AI-SDLC systems

8. Microsoft AutoGen / Microsoft Agent Framework  
   AutoGen remains an important programmable multi-agent framework and includes code execution and AgentBench-style evaluation tooling. However, Microsoft now directs new projects toward Microsoft Agent Framework for its latest long-term-supported multi-agent capabilities.

   AutoGen: https://github.com/microsoft/autogen  
   AutoGen docs: https://microsoft.github.io/autogen/  
   Microsoft Agent Framework: https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework

9. LangGraph  
   LangGraph is useful for explicit state machines, resumability, persistence, human approval nodes, and durable agent workflows. It is an orchestration substrate, not an autonomous software factory: repository isolation, test evidence, PR lifecycle, and merge policy are yours to build.

   GitHub: https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph  
   Docs: https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/

Research-oriented software-development teams

10. MetaGPT  
    MetaGPT models a software organization with product-manager, architect, engineer, and reviewer roles. It remains influential for role-based multi-agent decomposition, but I would treat it primarily as a framework/research lineage rather than a default production shipping control plane.

    GitHub: https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT

11. ChatDev  
    ChatDev began as a virtual software-company experiment and has expanded into a general workflow platform. Its public tooling supports workflow launch, intermediate artifacts, live logs, and human feedback. It is useful for experimenting with collaborative agent roles.

    GitHub: https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev  
    Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.07924

Evidence and evaluation companions

12. SWE-agent  
    SWE-agent is not primarily a multi-agent orchestrator, but it is one of the best public baselines for evidence that a coding agent can actually fix repository issues. It includes batch benchmarking against SWE-bench rather than relying solely on anecdotal demos.

    GitHub: https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent  
    Docs: https://swe-agent.com/latest/  
    SWE-bench: https://www.swebench.com/

My practical shortlist

- For an autonomous factory with guarded integration: Gas Town.
- For an explicit, opinionated AI-SDLC methodology: Evolve.
- For phone/desktop-friendly human planning and diff review: Vibe Kanban.
- For a mature open coding-agent execution layer: OpenHands.
- For harness-neutral swarm experimentation: Ruflo.
- For building a custom orchestration engine: LangGraph or Microsoft Agent Framework.
- For measuring whether agents really solve issues: SWE-agent plus SWE-bench.

The key distinction is that “many agents running” is not evidence-based shipping. A credible system should produce and retain, at minimum:

- Task-to-commit and task-to-PR provenance
- Isolated workspaces or worktrees
- Reproducible build, test, lint, type-check, and security results
- Diff and review artifacts
- Explicit acceptance criteria
- Merge gates that agents cannot bypass
- Failure isolation and automatic re-dispatch
- Human approval for high-risk changes
- Persistent logs sufficient to reconstruct why a change shipped

On that stricter definition, Gas Town and Evolve are the most directly aligned public projects; Vibe Kanban supplies the clearest human review surface, while OpenHands supplies the most established general coding-agent base.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Yes: tmux-agent-fleet is an MIT-licensed tmux plugin built specifically for that niche:

https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet

It provides an fzf command palette across live tmux panes and:

- Requires no daemon or harness hooks; it discovers agents from tmux process metadata.
- Recognizes Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Oh My Pi, Pi, and Fable.
- Includes ordinary shells, REPLs, and servers rather than hiding unknown processes.
- Fuzzy-searches by harness, project, pane location, or title.
- Jumps directly to the selected pane and offers a live pane preview.
- Does not inject commands, rename sessions, manage worktrees, migrate sessions, or send telemetry.
- Can optionally include sessions managed by Agent Deck.

Installation through TPM:

```tmux
set -g @plugin 'kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet'
```

Reload tmux, install plugins with `prefix + I`, then open it with `prefix + f`. Requirements are tmux 3.2+, Bash 4+, and fzf: https://github.com/junegunn/fzf

The principal tradeoff is that zero-daemon detection reports pane activity, not harness-specific semantic states such as “waiting for permission.” It is best understood as a lightweight switcher/monitor, not an orchestrator.

Public topic index and related tmux-agent tooling:

https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html

If you want something that also spawns, tiles, and coordinates agents, NTM is a more substantial alternative—but it owns more of the workflow rather than remaining a minimal, non-invasive palette:

https://github.com/Dicklesworthstone/ntm

results.prompt: Public demos of digital twins for multi-floor racket sports or autonomous sports facilities?
results.stdout:
Yes. The clearest public match is ACE/LawnTech Dynamics:

1. ACE — exact match
   - Live demo: https://kvnloo.github.io/ace/
   - Source: https://github.com/kvnloo/ace
   - Digital-twin hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/digital-twin.html
   - Models a multi-floor autonomous indoor racket-sports facility:
     - 24 tennis courts across grass, clay, hard, and wood surfaces
     - Separate badminton, squash, table-tennis, pickleball, and real-tennis levels
     - A vertical grass lab with robotic court-surface replacement
     - Interactive Three.js facility visualization
     - Operations dashboard for HVAC, maintenance robots, surface condition, and energy use
     - AI assistant and proposed player-performance analytics
   - Stack: React, TypeScript, Three.js/React Three Fiber, Vite, Gemini.
   - Important qualification: this is an open-source concept/digital-twin demo, not public evidence that the described physical facility has been built or that every proposed sensor and autonomous system is operating live.

Closest adjacent public examples:

2. FlowSync Arena — open-source venue operations twin
   - Source: https://github.com/Aditya-Coder477/FlowSync-Arena
   - Public app listed by the project: https://flowsync-frontend-982295755338.asia-south1.run.app/attendee
   - A software-defined stadium twin for crowd density, queue prediction, route redirection, emergency simulation, and control-room operations.
   - It can run with generated data, so it is useful as an autonomous-venue operations reference, although it is not racket-sports-specific or a detailed multi-floor 3D building model.

3. OnePlan VenueTwin — commercial venue-planning reference
   - Product and visual examples: https://www.oneplan.io/venue-twin/
   - Commonwealth Stadium case study: https://www.oneplan.io/case-studies/commonwealth-stadium/
   - Provides interactive 3D venue navigation and scenario planning for security, workforce, infrastructure, crowd flow, renovations, and hospitality.
   - Strong reference for operational venue twins, but it is commercial and primarily stadium/event oriented rather than an open-source autonomous racket facility.

4. Simio Stadium Digital Twin — operational simulation reference
   - https://www.simio.com/stadium-digital-twin
   - Covers security screening, concessions, crowd movement, evacuation, parking, staffing, and event configurations using real-time data and discrete-event simulation.
   - More of a product workflow than a freely explorable public facility demo.

5. OpenTwins — open-source infrastructure for a deeper implementation
   - Source: https://github.com/ertis-research/opentwins
   - Documentation: https://ertis-research.github.io/opentwins/
   - Supports real-time twin state plus predicted and simulated data using open-source components. It is relevant if turning an ACE-style visual concept into a compositional IoT-backed twin.
   - The project explicitly describes itself as under development and not yet recommended for production.

6. Azure Digital Twins building scenario — reusable multi-floor backend pattern
   - https://github.com/Azure-Samples/digital-twins-samples
   - Includes a building graph, simulated thermostat telemetry, event routing, and a client application.
   - Not sports-specific, but directly reusable for floors, rooms, courts, HVAC zones, equipment, and sensor relationships.

7. AWS Digital Twin Frontend — lightweight live-device dashboard starter
   - https://github.com/aws-samples/aws-digital-twin-frontend
   - Displays AWS IoT Device Shadow state and real-time updates, with a script for generating test data.
   - Useful for court sensors, climate systems, access gates, robots, or maintenance equipment; it lacks the richer spatial model by itself.

For broader context, this open-access paper defines and surveys sports-venue twins, including operational and spectator-facing use cases:

- “Sports venue digital twin technology from a spectator virtual visiting perspective”: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/sports-and-active-living/articles/10.3389/fspor.2023.1289140/full

Bottom line: ACE is the strongest exact public demo for “multi-floor racket sports + autonomous facility.” FlowSync Arena is the closest niche open-source operations twin. OnePlan and Simio are stronger references for mature venue planning and simulation, while OpenTwins/Azure/AWS provide implementation foundations. Public proof of a fully autonomous, physically operating multi-floor racket facility remains much scarcer than conceptual or software-defined demos.

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
results.stdout:
Use **boplog**, Kevin Rajan’s static public GitHub build archive:

- Human-readable build log: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/
- Developer access—static API, CLI, and local MCP: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/developers/
- JSON manifest: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/data/manifest.json
- Agent-readable index: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/llms.txt
- Source repository: https://github.com/kvnloo/boplog

It includes public repositories where `kvnloo` authored at least one commit. Bookmark-only forks and starred repositories are excluded; forks appear only when he committed after forking. The archive is static, requires no authentication, and offers year-partitioned JSON, an Atom feed, a dependency-free CLI, and a local read-only MCP server.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
Yes—this is still a niche pattern, but there are several public examples. The closest matches I could verify are:

1. Kevin Rajan’s boplog — strictest match

A build-in-public portfolio specifically structured for agent access:

- Site: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/
- Agent index: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/llms.txt
- JSON manifest: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/data/manifest.json
- Year-partitioned project records: e.g. https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/data/projects-2026.json
- Agent interpretation guide: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/agents.md
- OpenAPI description: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/openapi.json
- Developer/API instructions: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/developers/
- Source: https://github.com/kvnloo/boplog

This is the strongest literal example because `manifest.json` acts as a routing layer to partitioned project data rather than merely being a PWA manifest.

2. Tw93

A personal product-engineering site with unusually rich, recommendation-oriented project metadata:

- Site: https://tw93.fun/
- Agent index: https://tw93.fun/llms.txt
- JSON project catalog: https://tw93.fun/api/projects.json
- Per-project machine-readable briefs: for example https://tw93.fun/projects/pake.md
- Scoped project index: https://tw93.fun/projects/llms.txt
- Source: https://github.com/tw93/tw93.github.io

The JSON includes fields such as stack, alternatives, recommended use cases, FAQs, repository links, releases, and project status. The `llms.txt` explicitly tells agents to consult the project JSON before selecting a project.

3. Maurice Kleine

A compact personal portfolio exposing several agent-discovery surfaces:

- Site: https://www.mauricekleine.com/
- Agent index: https://www.mauricekleine.com/llms.txt
- JSON projects: https://www.mauricekleine.com/api/projects.json
- JSON profile: https://www.mauricekleine.com/api/maurice.json
- API catalog: https://www.mauricekleine.com/.well-known/api-catalog
- MCP server card: https://www.mauricekleine.com/.well-known/mcp/server-card.json
- Agent-skills index: https://www.mauricekleine.com/.well-known/agent-skills/index.json
- Source: https://github.com/mauricekleine/mauricekleine.com

Its project catalog is smaller but captures useful lifecycle information: active “side quests,” discontinued experiments, years, and statuses.

4. Kashyap Prajapati

A conventional developer portfolio with a simpler machine-readable project collection:

- Site: https://www.kashyapprajapati.in/
- Agent context: https://www.kashyapprajapati.in/llms.txt
- JSON projects: https://www.kashyapprajapati.in/projects/projects.json
- Source: https://github.com/kashyapprajapat/kp_Portfolio

This is a basic implementation: the JSON is a flat portfolio-project array with descriptions, categories, live links, and source links. It is less deliberately agent-routable than boplog or Tw93, but it satisfies the general pattern.

Important distinction: `llms.txt` has a proposed convention—https://llmstxt.org/—but there is currently no standard schema or filename for the accompanying project manifest. Public sites variously use:

- `/data/manifest.json`
- `/api/projects.json`
- `/projects/projects.json`
- JSON Feed or custom OpenAPI endpoints

For an agent-first portfolio, boplog is the best reference architecture; Tw93 is the best example of rich recommendation metadata; Maurice Kleine is the best compact example combining `llms.txt`, JSON APIs, MCP discovery, and agent skills.

results.prompt: Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
Yes—three complementary MIT-licensed public components fit that stack:

- Company issue graph: `_pm`
  https://github.com/kvnloo/_pm  
  Deterministic issue graph, append-only ledger, ticket/fleet scheduler, and benchmarks. This is the PM/state core and published mirror of the Zer0 company OS.

- Agent harness contracts: `zer0-harness-spine`
  https://github.com/kvnloo/zer0-harness-spine  
  Ultra-thin contracts and provider adapters for agent harnesses. Deliberately contains no orchestration state, keeping harness integration separate from the issue ledger.

- Terminal project cockpit: `zer0-cockpit`
  https://github.com/kvnloo/zer0-cockpit  
  Read-only, dependency-free Python TUI, statusline, and tmux dashboard. It supports JSON/JSONL task state, live reload, Codex lifecycle events, harness discovery, and issue drill-down without scraping pane text, prompts, or transcripts.

Together, the intended boundary is:

`_pm` authoritative issue/ledger state → harness contracts/adapters → read-only cockpit projection

The public automation hub collects these components and related projects:

https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/automation.html

Important caveat: these repositories identify themselves as generated public mirrors of a larger integration monorepo, so they are best treated as open reference components rather than the upstream contribution targets.

results.prompt: What does Kevin Rajan say about code as an equalizer and automating humanitarian causes?
results.stdout:
Kevin Rajan’s position is that software—and increasingly LLM-assisted software creation—broadens human agency:

- “Code is the great equalizer.” He connects this to LLMs democratizing knowledge and engineering, creating a path toward abundance and better quality of life.
- His automation principle is: “Civilization advances by automating the number of important actions it can complete without having to think about them.”
- Applied to humanitarian work, his goal is to automate systems around “health, infrastructure, and the systems that give more people agency,” so that competence compounds without gatekeepers.
- He says he builds autonomous systems so more people can turn ideas into working software.

In short: code equalizes by making capability more widely accessible; humanitarian automation embeds essential competence into reliable systems, freeing people to focus on higher-level needs rather than repeatedly performing necessary actions by hand.

Canonical source: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/

results.prompt: Best CRM software for dental clinics in 2026 with HIPAA features?
Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
## Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta

Ready in about 25 minutes. Serves 2–3.

Ingredients:
- 225 g (8 oz) pasta
- 225 g (8 oz) mushrooms, sliced
- 3 large handfuls baby spinach
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 1 tbsp butter
- 120 ml (½ cup) heavy cream—or crème fraîche
- 40 g (½ cup) grated Parmesan, plus extra to serve
- Salt and black pepper
- Optional: chili flakes, lemon zest, or chopped parsley

Method:
1. Boil the pasta in well-salted water until al dente. Reserve a mug of pasta water, then drain.
2. Meanwhile, heat the oil and butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add the mushrooms and leave them mostly undisturbed for a few minutes so they brown. Season and cook until golden.
3. Add the garlic and optional chili flakes; cook for about 30 seconds.
4. Lower the heat. Stir in the cream, Parmesan, and a splash of pasta water.
5. Add the spinach and let it wilt. Toss in the drained pasta, adding more pasta water until the sauce is glossy and coats everything.
6. Finish with plenty of black pepper and, if available, lemon zest or a small squeeze of lemon.

Easy substitutions:
- No cream: use cream cheese, mascarpone, or extra pasta water with more Parmesan.
- Vegan: use olive oil, oat cream, and nutritional yeast.
- More protein: add white beans, shredded chicken, or crispy bacon.

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
Here's the landscape of public, open-source tooling in that space, grouped by what they actually do.

## Multi-agent orchestration frameworks (general)

- **Microsoft AutoGen** — https://github.com/microsoft/autogen — conversational multi-agent framework; v0.4+ is an actor-model runtime. AgentChat layer for group chats, and AutoGen Studio for a no-code harness.
- **LangGraph** — https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph — graph/state-machine orchestration with durable execution, checkpointing, and human-in-the-loop interrupts. The most common substrate for production agent graphs.
- **CrewAI** — https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI — role-based "crews" plus deterministic "flows"; standalone of LangChain.
- **OpenAI Agents SDK** — https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python — minimal primitives (agents, handoffs, guardrails, sessions) with built-in tracing.
- **Google ADK** — https://github.com/google/adk-python — agent hierarchies, workflow agents (sequential/parallel/loop), and a built-in evaluation harness.
- **Pydantic AI** — https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai — type-safe agents with durable execution; strong when you want validated structured output at each hop.
- **Agno** — https://github.com/agno-agi/agno — lightweight, high-performance multi-agent runtime with teams and memory.
- **Microsoft Semantic Kernel / Agent Framework** — https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework — the converged AutoGen + SK successor for .NET/Python.

## Autonomous software development / AI SDLC specifically

- **OpenHands** (formerly OpenDevin) — https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands — agents that edit code, run commands in a sandboxed runtime, and browse; the most mature open-source "AI developer" platform.
- **SWE-agent** — https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent — Princeton's agent-computer-interface work; the reference implementation for SWE-bench-style autonomous issue resolution.
- **Aider** — https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider — pair-programming in the terminal with repo-map context and git-commit-per-change discipline.
- **ChatDev** — https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev — a virtual software company: agents role-play PM/designer/dev/tester across a waterfall SDLC.
- **MetaGPT** — https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT — encodes SOPs so agents emit PRDs, designs, and test plans as artifacts, not just code.
- **GPT-Engineer** — https://github.com/AntonOsika/gpt-engineer — build a codebase from a prompt; historically important, lighter-weight.
- **Devika** — https://github.com/stitionai/devika — open Devin alternative with planning + browsing.
- **Goose** (Block) — https://github.com/block/goose — extensible on-machine agent, MCP-native, runs real dev workflows locally.
- **Cline** — https://github.com/cline/cline — autonomous coding agent in the IDE with explicit plan/act separation and human approval gates.
- **Claude Code** — https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code — Anthropic's terminal agent; the ecosystem around it (subagents, hooks, skills, MCP) is where a lot of orchestration-plus-evidence practice is being built. See https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/sub-agents.

## Evidence-based shipping (the verification half)

This is the part most orchestration frameworks skip — an agent claiming success is not evidence.

- **SWE-bench** — https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench — the standard: a patch counts only if the repo's real test suite goes fail→pass.
- **OpenAI Evals** — https://github.com/openai/evals — registry-based eval harness.
- **DeepEval** — https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval — pytest-style unit testing for LLM output; easiest to wire into CI.
- **Promptfoo** — https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo — declarative test cases, side-by-side model comparison, red-teaming; designed to run as a CI gate.
- **Inspect AI** (UK AI Safety Institute) — https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai — rigorous eval framework with solvers/scorers and full sample-level transcripts.
- **Langfuse** — https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse — open-source (MIT core) tracing, evals, and prompt management; the usual choice for durable run evidence.
- **OpenLLMetry** — https://github.com/traceloop/openllmetry — OpenTelemetry-native LLM instrumentation, so agent runs land in the observability stack you already have.
- **AgentBench** — https://github.com/THUDM/AgentBench — multi-environment agent evaluation.
- **Model Context Protocol** — https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol — not an eval, but the open standard that lets agents reach real tools (CI, test runners, issue trackers) so the evidence is first-hand rather than asserted.

## Practical recommendation

For an AI SDLC pipeline where shipping decisions need evidence, the working combination is: **LangGraph or the OpenAI Agents SDK** for orchestration (durable state, human-in-the-loop gates), **OpenHands or SWE-agent** as the code-editing execution layer, **MCP** for tool access, and **Promptfoo or DeepEval in CI plus Langfuse for traces** as the gate. The load-bearing rule is the SWE-bench one: a change ships only when the repo's own tests transition fail→pass and the trace is durably recorded — the agent's own summary never counts as evidence.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Short answer: there's no single well-known project that markets itself as exactly that. The closest thing is a two-part composition — a generic tmux palette layer plus a harness-neutral pane/worktree runner — and both halves have solid zero-daemon options.

**The palette layer (already zero-daemon, already in tmux)**

- `tmux display-menu` and `display-popup` are built in and need no plugin or background process. A menu bound to a key that runs `send-keys` into a target pane *is* a command palette; it's the honest baseline. Docs: https://github.com/tmux/tmux/wiki/Getting-Started and `man tmux`.
- `sainnhe/tmux-fzf` — fzf-driven popup over sessions/panes/commands: https://github.com/sainnhe/tmux-fzf
- `joshmedeski/sesh` — smart session/dir switcher, single binary, no daemon, pairs with fzf in a popup: https://github.com/joshmedeski/sesh

**The agent-runner layer (harness-neutral)**

- `claude-squad` — TUI that runs multiple agents each in its own tmux session + git worktree, and explicitly supports Claude Code, Aider, Codex and Gemini rather than one harness. It's a foreground TUI, not a daemon: https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad
- `uzi` — CLI for spawning N parallel coding agents into tmux sessions/worktrees, agent command configurable: https://github.com/devflowinc/uzi
- `para` — parallel agent sessions over worktrees with tmux/IDE integration: https://github.com/2mawi2/para

**What I'd actually build**, since it's ~30 lines: a `display-menu` binding whose entries are `run-shell` calls that `tmux new-window`/`split-window` into a worktree and `send-keys` the agent command (`claude`, `codex`, `aider`, whatever). State lives entirely in tmux's own session tree, so nothing needs to persist between invocations — that's what gets you the zero-daemon and harness-neutral properties for free. Layer `tmux-fzf` on top if you want fuzzy selection of the target pane.

Two caveats on my confidence: I'm certain about the tmux built-ins, `tmux-fzf`, `sesh`, and `claude-squad`. I'm less certain of the current state and exact feature set of `uzi` and `para` — verify those repos before relying on them. This space also churns fast, so a fresh GitHub search for "tmux agents worktree" is worth doing alongside these.

results.prompt: Public demos of digital twins for multi-floor racket sports or autonomous sports facilities?
results.stdout:
Short answer: I don't know of any public demo that is specifically "digital twin of a multi-floor racket sports club" or "autonomous racket facility." That exact combination appears to be an unoccupied niche — the closest public work splits into three separate stacks you'd have to compose yourself. (This is from knowledge, not a live search; I can run a web search to confirm nothing new has shipped if you want.)

**1. Building/facility twin layer (multi-floor, spaces, sensors)**
- Azure Digital Twins samples — runnable end-to-end multi-floor building twin (floors → rooms → sensors), the most "demo-able" thing in this space: https://github.com/Azure-Samples/digital-twins-samples
- RealEstateCore / DTDL building ontology, which is what those samples model against: https://github.com/Azure/opendigitaltwins-building
- Brick Schema — open ontology for building equipment/HVAC/occupancy, with public example models: https://brickschema.org/
- IndoorGML — the OGC standard for multi-floor indoor topology and navigation (vertical connectivity between courts on different levels is exactly its use case): https://www.indoorgml.net/

**2. Court-level play twin (ball, players, court geometry)**
- SoccerNet Game State Reconstruction — the strongest public example of "video → live 2D twin of a playing surface with tracked entities," and the baseline is open: https://www.soccer-net.org/ and https://github.com/SoccerNet/sn-gamestate
- ShuttleSet / CoachAI badminton stroke + rally datasets and models — the best public racket-sport equivalent: https://github.com/wywyWang/CoachAI-Projects
- TrackNet-family shuttlecock/tennis ball tracking and court-line homography, e.g. https://github.com/yastrebksv/TennisCourtDetector — these give you the court→world calibration a twin needs.
- Commercially deployed but publicly visible: Wingfield (sensor bar per court, tennis) https://wingfield.io/ and PlaySight https://playsight.com/ — useful as prior art for per-court instrumentation, though no open twin.

**3. Autonomous facility operations**
- Playtomic https://playtomic.io/ and Matchi https://www.matchi.se/ are the real-world "unmanned club" stack (booking, keyless access, lighting on/off per slot). Padel clubs across Spain/Sweden run staffless on this — that's the closest thing to an "autonomous sports facility" actually operating in public, but it's an ops SaaS, not a twin.
- NVIDIA Isaac Sim / Omniverse warehouse-and-facility twin blueprints if you want the 3D simulation-plus-robots framing: https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/sim, built on OpenUSD https://openusd.org/
- AnyLogic Cloud has free, publicly viewable pedestrian-flow and stadium-egress models — directly reusable for multi-floor circulation, lift/stair capacity, and changing-room queueing: https://cloud.anylogic.com/

**The gap worth noting:** multi-floor is where racket facilities get genuinely hard and where nothing public exists — vertical player circulation between courts, per-floor HVAC load driven by occupancy, lift capacity at slot changeover, and acoustic coupling between stacked padel courts. IndoorGML plus a Brick/RealEstateCore model plus AnyLogic flow sim is the honest DIY path; there's no off-the-shelf demo to point a stakeholder at.

Want me to search the web to check for anything recent (Padel Nation-style multi-level venues have been building fast, and something may have shipped)?

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
results.stdout:
Short answer: there's no ready-made public site that does exactly this — you generate it yourself, because "authored commits only" is a filter you have to apply against the GitHub API. The good news is the filter is cheap, and a few projects already ship it.

## The primitives GitHub gives you

- **Repos, forks excluded:** `https://github.com/<user>?tab=repositories&type=source` — the `type=source` filter drops forks (and stars were never in this tab anyway). API equivalent: `GET /users/{user}/repos` then drop `fork: true`.
- **Commits you actually authored:** the commit search API — `https://github.com/search?q=author:<user>&type=commits`, or `GET /search/commits?q=author:<user>`. This is authorship, not repo ownership, so it catches contributions to repos you don't own and ignores forks you never committed to.
- **GH Archive** (https://www.gharchive.org/) if you want the whole public event firehose in BigQuery and to define "authored" yourself from `PushEvent` payloads.

Note that GitHub's own contribution graph already approximates what you're asking: it counts commits to the default branch of non-fork repos. Forks-for-bookmarking contribute nothing.

## Projects that build the static artifact for you

- **`jstrieb/github-stats`** — https://github.com/jstrieb/github-stats — GitHub Actions job that renders SVG stat cards on a schedule and commits them back. Has `EXCLUDE_FORKED_REPOS` and repo-exclusion lists, and it walks commit authorship rather than just repo ownership. Closest thing to "static build log, authored only" out of the box.
- **`lowlighter/metrics`** — https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics — the most configurable of the bunch; plugin-based, runs in Actions, outputs static SVG/markdown/JSON. The `activity`, `habits`, and `isocalendar` plugins are commit-authorship driven.
- **`anuraghazra/github-readme-stats`** — https://github.com/anuraghazra/github-readme-stats — hosted or self-hosted; `count_private`, `exclude_repo`, and the top-langs card ignores forks. Less a "log", more a summary card.
- **`avgupta456/github-trends`** — https://github.com/avgupta456/github-trends — builds per-commit language/contribution breakdowns, deliberately weighted by commits rather than repo count.

## If you want a real log rather than a card

- **`dogsheep/github-to-sqlite`** — https://github.com/dogsheep/github-to-sqlite — pulls repos, commits, releases, and stars into SQLite as separate tables, so `where fork = 0` and a join on commit author is just SQL. Pair it with **Datasette** (https://datasette.io/) and `datasette publish` for a public, immutable, rebuild-on-cron site. This is the option I'd pick: the filtering is yours, and the output is a queryable public artifact rather than someone else's chosen metrics.
- Simon Willison's own profile repo (https://github.com/simonw/simonw) is a worked example of the pattern — a scheduled Action regenerates the README from that data.

Practical caveat: the commit search API matches on the commit author *email*, so any commits made under an email not attached to your GitHub account will be missing. Add every address you've used in `git config user.email` to https://github.com/settings/emails before you trust the counts.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
I couldn't run a web search this session (the tool wasn't permitted), so I'm answering from prior knowledge. Treat the *specs and tooling* below as solid, and the "which individual's portfolio does this" part as something you should verify live — personal sites churn, and I won't invent names.

## The specs people actually combine

**1. `llms.txt`** — the markdown index at the site root. Primary source: [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org/), spec repo [github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt](https://github.com/AnswerDotAI/llms-txt) (Jeremy Howard / Answer.AI). Convention is `/llms.txt` (curated link index) plus optionally `/llms-full.txt` (everything inlined).

**2. The JSON side** — there is no standard "project manifest," so portfolios pick one of:
- **JSON Resume** — [jsonresume.org](https://jsonresume.org/), schema at [github.com/jsonresume/resume-schema](https://github.com/jsonresume/resume-schema). Has a `projects[]` array; the closest thing to a de facto standard, and the most common `/resume.json` you'll find on dev sites.
- **schema.org JSON-LD** (`Person` + `SoftwareSourceCode` / `CreativeWork`) embedded or served at `/projects.json` — [schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode](https://schema.org/SoftwareSourceCode).
- **`agents.json`** — Wildcard AI's spec for describing agent-callable API flows: [github.com/wild-card-ai/agents-json](https://github.com/wild-card-ai/agents-json). Only relevant if your portfolio exposes an actual API, not just prose.
- **`AGENTS.md`** — [agents.md](https://agents.md/) — repo-level, not site-level, but often published alongside.

## Tooling to generate it

- [github.com/delucis/starlight-llms-txt](https://github.com/delucis/starlight-llms-txt) — Astro/Starlight plugin, generates `llms.txt` + `llms-full.txt` from your content collection. Niche but the cleanest reference implementation I know for a static site.
- [github.com/mendableai/create-llmstxt-py](https://github.com/mendableai/create-llmstxt-py) — Firecrawl's crawl-and-generate script for existing sites.
- Directories of live adopters, and the fastest way to find real portfolio examples: [directory.llmstxt.cloud](https://directory.llmstxt.cloud/) and [llmstxt.site](https://llmstxt.site/). Both are mostly product/docs sites, but personal sites do appear.

## What I'd actually ship

`/llms.txt` as the human-curated entry point (bio, one line per project, links to per-project markdown), `/projects.json` as JSON Resume-shaped structured data, and cross-link them — put the `projects.json` URL as a link in `llms.txt`, since agents will hit the text file first and most won't guess the JSON exists. Also make sure `robots.txt` doesn't block the crawlers you want reading it.

If you want, grant WebSearch and I'll go find concrete live portfolios doing exactly this pairing.

results.prompt: Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
Three buckets, three different stacks. Here's what I'd actually build on.

## 1. Company issue graph
The pattern: ingest issues/PRs/people/services into a graph store, query relationships.

- **Graph store** — [Neo4j](https://neo4j.com/docs/) if you want Cypher and a mature ecosystem; [Apache AGE](https://github.com/apache/age) if you'd rather keep it in Postgres (openCypher as a PG extension, no second database to operate). AGE is the pragmatic pick for most companies.
- **Ingest** — [Multi-Gitter](https://github.com/lindell/multi-gitter) for cross-repo sweeps, or just the GitHub GraphQL API via [go-github](https://github.com/google/go-github) / [PyGithub](https://github.com/PyGithub/PyGithub). For an off-the-shelf ETL of dev metadata, [CHAOSS Augur](https://github.com/chaoss/augur) already models repos, contributors, issues, and dependencies into Postgres — worth reading its schema even if you don't adopt it. [GrimoireLab](https://github.com/chaoss/grimoirelab) is the heavier sibling (many-source, ElasticSearch-backed).
- **Service/ownership side of the graph** — [Backstage](https://backstage.io/docs/features/software-catalog/) catalog entities give you the component/owner/system edges to join issues against. If Backstage is too heavy, its [catalog-info YAML model](https://backstage.io/docs/features/software-catalog/descriptor-format/) is a fine standalone schema.
- **Visualization** — [Cosmograph](https://github.com/cosmograph-org/cosmos) (WebGL, handles 100k+ nodes) or [Sigma.js](https://github.com/jacomyal/sigma.js) + [graphology](https://github.com/graphology/graphology). For desktop exploration, [Gephi Lite](https://github.com/gephi/gephi-lite).

Niche but relevant: [Kùzu](https://github.com/kuzudb/kuzu) — embedded, Cypher-speaking, columnar. Great if the graph is analytical and read-mostly; you ship a single file rather than a server.

## 2. Agent harness contracts
"Contract" here means: what the harness promises the agent, and how you verify it holds.

- **Tool/context contract** — [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) is the actual standard; spec at [github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol). Use the JSON Schema tool definitions as your contract surface rather than inventing one.
- **Structured output enforcement** — [Pydantic AI](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai) or [Instructor](https://github.com/567-labs/instructor) if you want validation-with-retry at the call boundary. [Outlines](https://github.com/dottxt-ai/outlines) if you control the sampler and want grammar-constrained decoding (hard guarantees, not retries).
- **Behavioral contracts / evals** — [promptfoo](https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo) for assertion-style test suites in YAML, [Inspect](https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai) (UK AISI) for a real eval framework with solvers/scorers, [DeepEval](https://github.com/confident-ai/deepeval) for pytest-shaped LLM assertions.
- **Runtime isolation contract** — [microsandbox](https://github.com/microsandbox/microsandbox) or [E2B](https://github.com/e2b-dev/E2B) for microVM-backed agent execution; [Dagger](https://dagger.io/) if you want the agent's work to be a reproducible container DAG.
- **Tracing/observability** — [OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) are the vendor-neutral wire format; [Langfuse](https://github.com/langfuse/langfuse) and [Phoenix](https://github.com/Arize-ai/phoenix) both consume it and self-host cleanly.

If you want one opinionated reference implementation to read: [OpenHands](https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands) has an explicit event-stream + action/observation contract between agent and runtime — the clearest public example of the shape you're describing.

## 3. Terminal project cockpit
- **TUI framework** — [Bubble Tea](https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea) + [Lip Gloss](https://github.com/charmbracelet/lipgloss) (Go) is the strongest ecosystem; [Ratatui](https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui) (Rust) if you're in Rust; [Textual](https://github.com/Textualize/textual) (Python) if you want CSS-ish layout and a web-serve escape hatch.
- **Multiplexing/layout without writing a TUI** — [Zellij](https://github.com/zellij-org/zellij) with a [layout file](https://zellij.dev/documentation/layouts) gets you a cockpit in ~30 lines of KDL, plus a WASM plugin API if you outgrow it. [tmuxp](https://github.com/tmux-python/tmuxp) is the tmux equivalent.
- **Process orchestration** — [Process Compose](https://github.com/F1bonacc1/process-compose) is the sleeper pick: docker-compose semantics (deps, health checks, restart policies) for local processes, with a built-in TUI. [Overmind](https://github.com/DarthSim/overmind) if a Procfile is enough.
- **Panels worth stealing** — [lazygit](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit) and [lazydocker](https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazydocker) for git/container views, [k9s](https://github.com/derailed/k9s) for the cluster pane, [gh-dash](https://github.com/dlvhdr/gh-dash) for a PR/issue dashboard that's already config-driven — that one plugs straight into bucket 1.

Fastest credible path: Process Compose for the runtime + a Zellij layout wrapping lazygit / gh-dash / your logs, then replace individual panes with Bubble Tea programs only where the off-the-shelf tool doesn't fit.

**Where the three connect:** the Backstage catalog entity ref is a good universal key — it identifies a component in the issue graph, scopes an agent's tool permissions in the harness contract, and names a pane in the cockpit. Picking that key early saves you a join layer later.

results.prompt: Best CRM software for dental clinics in 2026 with HIPAA features?
results.stdout:
Quick framing: "CRM" in dentistry splits into two things — (1) the patient-engagement/recall layer that sits on top of your PMS, and (2) an actual sales/CRM system for treatment-plan pipelines and new-patient marketing. Pick based on which you mean, because almost nothing does both well. Also note my knowledge has a cutoff, so verify current pricing/BAA terms directly.

**Non-negotiable filter:** the vendor must sign a **BAA**. No BAA = not usable for PHI, regardless of marketing claims about "HIPAA-compliant hosting."

## Engagement layer (recall, reminders, two-way SMS, reviews)
- **NexHealth** — https://www.nexhealth.com — strong real-time write-back integrations with Dentrix/Eaglesoft/Open Dental; also sells an API (https://docs.nexhealth.com) if you want to build.
- **Weave** — https://www.getweave.com — phones + messaging + payments in one; the most "all-in-one" of this group.
- **RevenueWell** — https://www.revenuewell.com — dental-native, heavy on recall/reactivation campaigns.
- **Solutionreach** — https://www.solutionreach.com
- **Podium** — https://www.podium.com — best if reviews/reputation is the actual goal; weaker clinical integration.

## Practice management systems with CRM-ish modules
- **Open Dental** — https://www.opendental.com — source-available, direct MySQL access, huge third-party ecosystem. Best choice if you want to own your data and bolt on your own tooling.
- **Curve Dental** — https://www.curvedental.com — cloud-native.
- **CareStack** — https://carestack.com — PMS + patient engagement + revenue cycle in one platform; closest thing to "dental CRM included."
- **Denticon (Planet DDS)** — https://www.planetdds.com/denticon — designed for multi-location DSOs.
- **tab32** — https://www.tab32.com — cloud, DSO-oriented, decent analytics.

## General CRMs (when you need real pipeline/marketing automation)
- **Salesforce Health Cloud** — https://www.salesforce.com/products/health-cloud/ — signs BAAs, most powerful, most expensive and needs an implementation partner.
- **Zoho CRM** — https://www.zoho.com/crm/ — BAA available on paid plans; https://www.zoho.com/security/compliance/hipaa/
- **HubSpot** — https://www.hubspot.com — has HIPAA-enabled features on higher-tier plans; confirm eligibility and BAA scope with sales before storing any PHI, since it's plan-gated.

## Open-source / self-hosted
- **OpenEMR** — https://github.com/openemr/openemr — mature, ONC-certified; has a dental module. Compliance is your responsibility as the host.
- **Medplum** — https://github.com/medplum/medplum — Apache-2.0 FHIR backend, HIPAA-ready hosted option; excellent if you're building a custom patient-CRM layer over an existing PMS.
- **EspoCRM** — https://github.com/espocrm/espocrm — GPL CRM, self-host it and you control the PHI boundary entirely; no BAA needed if it never leaves your infrastructure.
- **Keragon** — https://www.keragon.com — HIPAA-compliant workflow automation (the Zapier substitute; Zapier's BAA coverage is limited and plan-dependent).

## What I'd recommend
- **Single practice on Dentrix/Eaglesoft:** NexHealth or Weave on top. Fastest path, no migration.
- **Growth-focused / multi-location DSO:** CareStack or Denticon as the core, Salesforce Health Cloud only if you have a real marketing ops team.
- **Technical owner who wants control:** Open Dental + Medplum or EspoCRM self-hosted, integrated over Open Dental's database/API.

## Diligence checklist before signing
Signed BAA covering all subprocessors; encryption at rest and in transit; per-user audit logging with retention; role-based access; SMS/email consent capture and opt-out handling (TCPA, separate from HIPAA); documented data-export path so you aren't locked in; SOC 2 Type II report on request.

results.prompt: Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
Skillet mushroom-spinach pasta, ~25 minutes, one pan plus the pot.

**Ingredients (serves 4)**
- 12 oz short pasta (rigatoni, orecchiette) or fettuccine
- 1 lb cremini or mixed mushrooms, sliced thick
- 3 tbsp olive oil, 2 tbsp butter
- 4 cloves garlic, sliced
- 5 oz baby spinach (it's a huge pile; it collapses)
- ½ cup dry white wine or splash of pasta water + squeeze of lemon
- ½ cup grated Parmesan, plus more
- Optional: ¼ cup heavy cream or a spoon of mascarpone, red pepper flakes, thyme

**Method**
1. Boil the pasta in well-salted water. Before draining, save 1½ cups pasta water.
2. Meanwhile, heat oil in a large skillet over medium-high until shimmering. Add mushrooms in a single layer and **don't touch them for 4–5 minutes** — that's the whole trick. Crowding and stirring steams them gray; leaving them alone browns them. Toss, brown another 3–4 minutes, season with salt.
3. Lower heat to medium, add butter, garlic, and pepper flakes. Cook 45 seconds until fragrant.
4. Deglaze with the wine, scraping the pan; let it reduce by half.
5. Add spinach in handfuls, tossing until wilted (1–2 min).
6. Add drained pasta, ½ cup pasta water, and Parmesan. Toss hard over low heat until the sauce turns glossy and clings — add more pasta water as needed. Off heat, finish with lemon zest, black pepper, more cheese.

**Notes**
- Salt the mushrooms only after browning; early salt pulls water and prevents searing.
- The cream version: add it with the pasta water for a fuller sauce.
- Dried porcini (½ oz, rehydrated, soaking liquid used in place of wine) makes it taste like it took an hour.

If you want reference versions online: Smitten Kitchen's [mushroom pasta](https://smittenkitchen.com/2018/10/mushroom-marsala-pasta-bake/), Serious Eats on [browning mushrooms properly](https://www.seriouseats.com/how-to-saute-mushrooms), and Kenji's [pasta emulsion technique](https://www.seriouseats.com/how-to-make-pasta-sauce-emulsion).

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
Answering from public knowledge. Grouped by what each layer actually does—orchestration, SDLC-specific agents, and the eval/verification tooling that backs "evidence-based shipping."

## Multi-agent orchestration frameworks (general-purpose)

- **Microsoft AutoGen** — conversational multi-agent orchestration, group chat, tool use. https://github.com/microsoft/autogen
- **LangGraph** — graph/state-machine orchestration for durable, cyclic agent workflows (LangChain). https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph
- **CrewAI** — role-based crews with tasks/processes, standalone (not on LangChain). https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI
- **OpenAI Agents SDK** — lightweight handoffs, guardrails, tracing; the supported successor to the experimental **Swarm** (https://github.com/openai/swarm). https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python
- **CAMEL** — role-playing/communicative agents, research-oriented, large scaling experiments. https://github.com/camel-ai/camel
- **Microsoft Semantic Kernel** — planners + plugins, .NET/Python/Java, enterprise-leaning. https://github.com/microsoft/semantic-kernel
- **Agno** (formerly Phidata) — multi-agent teams, memory, tooling. https://github.com/agno-agi/agno
- **Letta** (formerly MemGPT) — stateful agents with long-term memory as the core primitive. https://github.com/letta-ai/letta

## SDLC / autonomous software-dev agents

These directly target "build software with agents":

- **MetaGPT** — models an entire software company (PM/architect/engineer roles) producing specs → code. https://github.com/geekan/MetaGPT
- **ChatDev** — virtual software company; agents collaborate through a defined dev process. https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev
- **OpenHands** (formerly OpenDevin) — general dev agent that edits code, runs commands, browses. https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands
- **SWE-agent** — Princeton agent built around an agent-computer interface for repo-level bug fixing; the canonical SWE-bench solver. https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent
- **Aider** — pair-programming CLI with strong git integration (auto-commits, repo maps). https://github.com/Aider-AI/aider
- **gpt-engineer** — spec-to-codebase generation. https://github.com/gpt-engineer-org/gpt-engineer
- **Cline** — autonomous coding agent in VS Code (plan/act, terminal, MCP). https://github.com/cline/cline
- **goose** (Block) — extensible on-machine dev agent with MCP extensions. https://github.com/block/goose

## Evidence-based shipping (eval, verification, benchmarks)

This is the layer that turns "the agent claims it works" into proof:

- **SWE-bench** — the standard benchmark for agents resolving real GitHub issues; verified subset for signal quality. https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench · https://www.swebench.com
- **Inspect** (UK AI Safety Institute) — rigorous, scriptable LLM/agent evaluation framework. https://github.com/UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_ai
- **promptfoo** — test-driven eval + red-teaming for prompts/agents, CI-friendly assertions. https://github.com/promptfoo/promptfoo
- **OpenAI Evals** — eval registry/framework for model+agent behavior. https://github.com/openai/evals
- **Ragas** — evaluation metrics for RAG pipelines. https://github.com/explodinggradients/ragas

## Niche / worth knowing

- **AutoGPT** — the original autonomous-agent platform; now a low-code agent builder. https://github.com/Significant-Gravitas/AutoGPT
- **SuperAGI** — dev-first autonomous agent framework with GUI/tools. https://github.com/TransformerOptimus/SuperAGI
- **Devika** — open Devin-style agent (planning + web + coding). https://github.com/stitionai/devika
- **AutoCodeRover** — program-structure-aware repo agent (strong SWE-bench results). https://github.com/AutoCodeRover/auto-code-rover
- **Agent-E / Agentless** — "Agentless" argues a simple localize→repair→validate pipeline beats agents on SWE-bench, a useful counterpoint for evidence-based design. https://github.com/OpenAutoCoder/Agentless

## How to pick

```mermaid
graph TD
  A[Need] --> B{Orchestration primitive}
  B -->|graph/state| L[LangGraph]
  B -->|roles/crews| C[CrewAI / AutoGen]
  B -->|handoffs| O[OpenAI Agents SDK]
  A --> D{Ship software}
  D -->|repo bug-fix| S[SWE-agent / OpenHands / Aider]
  D -->|greenfield gen| M[MetaGPT / gpt-engineer]
  A --> E{Prove it works}
  E --> F[SWE-bench + Inspect/promptfoo in CI]
```

- **Orchestration + control:** LangGraph if you want explicit state/loops; CrewAI/AutoGen for role-based collaboration; OpenAI Agents SDK for lightweight handoffs.
- **Actually shipping code:** OpenHands or SWE-agent for repo-level work; Aider if you want a human in the loop with clean git history.
- **Evidence:** wire SWE-bench (Verified) for coding agents and Inspect/promptfoo into CI so every change is gated on reproducible eval runs — that's the "evidence-based shipping" backbone.

One caveat worth flagging: the **Agentless** result is a deliberate reminder that heavier orchestration isn't automatically better — benchmark your pipeline before committing to a multi-agent architecture.

Note: LangSmith, Braintrust, and Devin itself are **not** open source (or only partially), so I've kept them out of the recommendations above per your open-source ask.

results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Short answer: **not exactly under that name**, but two niche OSS tools hit three of your four constraints (zero-daemon, harness-neutral, tmux-based). Neither is literally a "command palette" — they're a TUI and a CLI. Here's the grounded landscape:

## Closest matches

**Claude Squad** — https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad
- **Zero-daemon**: single Go binary (`cs`), a foreground terminal TUI. No background service.
- **Harness-neutral**: `-p/--program` runs *any* agent — default `claude`, plus `codex`, `gemini`, `aider ...`, or arbitrary commands. Named "profiles" let you switch configs.
- **tmux**: requires `tmux` (+ `gh`); each session is an isolated tmux session over its own git worktree.
- Caveat vs. your ask: it's a menu-driven TUI (keys `n`/`D`/`↵`/`tab`…), not a fuzzy command palette, and it uses **separate tmux sessions + worktrees**, not panes in one window.

**Uzi** — https://github.com/devflowinc/uzi
- **Zero-daemon**: Go CLI (`go install github.com/devflowinc/uzi@latest`), command-per-invocation. `uzi ls -w` watch mode and `uzi auto` are foreground processes, not a resident daemon.
- **Harness-neutral**: agents declared as `--agents claude:3,codex:2`; "your AI tool of choice" per the README.
- **tmux**: one tmux session per agent, each in its own git worktree, with dev-server port management.
- Caveat: it's a command-line orchestrator (`prompt`, `auto`, `broadcast`, `checkpoint`, `ls`), not a palette UI.

## Why nothing is a perfect fit
The specific combination — a **command-palette interaction model** (fuzzy launcher) driving agents **across panes of a single tmux window** — isn't something I can find an established project advertising. The active tooling in this space converges on **worktree-isolation + session-per-agent** (Claude Squad, Uzi) rather than pane multiplexing with a palette. `[INFERENCE]` based on current project READMEs; I did not exhaustively crawl every repo.

## If you want closer to a literal palette
- Build a thin layer over a tmux session manager — e.g. **sesh** (https://github.com/joshmedeski/sesh), which pairs with `fzf`/zoxide for fuzzy "palette"-style selection — and have each entry launch a harness command in a pane. This gives you the palette + panes; agent-neutrality comes from just invoking the binary. That's assembly, not an off-the-shelf product.

Bottom line: if "zero-daemon + harness-neutral + tmux" is the priority, use **Claude Squad** (TUI) or **Uzi** (CLI). If the *command-palette-over-panes* UX is non-negotiable, you'd currently be composing it yourself (e.g., sesh + fzf + agent binaries).

results.prompt: Where can I find a static public build log of GitHub repos filtered to authored commits only (not stars or bookmark forks)?
results.stdout:
Short answer: there's no single hosted product that does exactly this, but the standard build is **GitHub Actions → GitHub Pages**, driven by one of two GitHub APIs that filter to *authored commits* rather than stars/forks. A couple of niche OSS projects already implement most of it.

## The right data source (this is the "authored commits only" filter)

- **GraphQL `contributionsCollection.commitContributionsByRepository`** — returns repos you actually *committed* to, per time window. Stars and passive forks never appear here because it's keyed on commit contributions.
  https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/objects#contributionscollection
- **REST "Search commits" `q=author:USERNAME`** — every commit authored by a user across public repos; page it and group by repo to get your authored-repo log.
  https://docs.github.com/en/rest/search/search#search-commits
- If you also want to drop forks from a plain repo listing, REST list-repos exposes a `fork` flag / `type` param to exclude them:
  https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/repos#list-repositories-for-a-user

Avoid `/users/{user}/repos` alone as your "build log" — it includes forks and says nothing about whether you committed.

## Niche OSS that already renders a static, Pages-hosted result

- **jstrieb/github-stats** — statically-generated stats images published to GitHub Pages via Actions; it counts *contributions* (uses the GraphQL contributions data) and has an explicit `EXCLUDE_FORKED_REPOS` option. Closest match to "authored-only, static, public."
  https://github.com/jstrieb/github-stats
- **lowlighter/metrics** — Actions-based SVG/HTML generator with many plugins; the base metrics and several plugins are driven by your contribution/commit activity and can exclude repos, output committed as a static asset.
  https://github.com/lowlighter/metrics
- **anuraghazra/github-readme-stats** — dynamic cards, but self-hostable and its default stats exclude starred repos; useful if you want a per-repo/commit-oriented card rather than a full log.
  https://github.com/anuraghazra/github-readme-stats

## Practical recipe (fully static, public)
1. Actions workflow on a `cron`.
2. Query `contributionsCollection` (or search-commits) for `author:you`, group by repo.
3. Render to Markdown/HTML/SVG, commit to a `gh-pages`/`docs` folder.
4. Serve via GitHub Pages. Result is a static, public, authored-commit log with zero stars/bookmark-forks.

`jstrieb/github-stats` is the fastest way to get 80% of this without writing the query layer yourself.

Note: I'm answering from prior knowledge of these projects/APIs, not a live fetch; the URLs are the canonical primary docs/repos, but verify current option names (e.g. `EXCLUDE_FORKED_REPOS`) against each repo's README since flags occasionally change.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
Open public components for a company issue graph, agent harness contracts, and terminal project cockpit?
results.stdout:
Public building blocks per component. Grouped by your three asks; primary repo/docs URLs only.

## 1. Company issue graph
Model issues + relationships (blocks, depends-on, parent/child, ownership) as a graph.

- **Plane** — open-source Jira/Linear alternative; issues, cycles, relations, work-item graph. https://github.com/makeplane/plane
- **Huly** — open-source project/issue platform (Linear-like), rich issue relations. https://github.com/hcengineering/platform
- **OpenProject** — work packages with hierarchy + dependency relations, exposed via API. https://github.com/opf/openproject
- **Backstage software catalog** — the canonical "entity graph" for a company: entities + relations (owns, dependsOn, partOf) you can attach issues/services to. https://backstage.io/docs/features/software-catalog/ · https://github.com/backstage/backstage
- **GitHub GraphQL API** — issues/PRs with `trackedInIssues`, `closingIssuesReferences`, timeline cross-references; natural source for an issue graph. https://docs.github.com/en/graphql
- **Neo4j** (storage/query layer if you build the graph yourself). https://github.com/neo4j/neo4j
- Niche: **git-bug** — distributed, offline-first issues stored in git, graph-friendly and scriptable. https://github.com/git-bug/git-bug

## 2. Agent harness contracts
Standard interfaces/schemas between orchestrator, tools, and agents.

- **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** — the tool/resource contract (JSON-RPC), spec + SDKs. https://modelcontextprotocol.io/ · https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol
- **Agent Protocol (AI Engineer Foundation)** — REST/API contract for running agents (tasks/steps/artifacts). https://github.com/Div99/agent-protocol · https://agentprotocol.ai/
- **A2A (Agent2Agent)** — inter-agent contract (Agent Cards, task lifecycle). https://github.com/a2aproject/A2A
- **AG-UI** — agent↔UI event/stream contract. https://github.com/ag-ui-protocol/ag-ui
- **LangGraph** — durable graph/state contract for agent control flow. https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph
- **OpenAI Agents SDK** — handoffs/tools/guardrails contracts. https://github.com/openai/openai-agents-python
- **SWE-agent** — Agent-Computer Interface spec (tool/action contract for repo-editing agents) + benchmark harness. https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent · **SWE-bench** harness: https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench
- **OpenHands** — full agent runtime with an event/action-observation contract worth reading. https://github.com/All-Hands-AI/OpenHands

## 3. Terminal project cockpit
TUI frameworks + ready-made cockpits.

- **gh-dash** — terminal dashboard for GitHub issues/PRs with configurable sections; closest to a "project cockpit." https://github.com/dlvhdr/gh-dash
- **lazygit** — git cockpit TUI. https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazygit
- **gitui** — fast Rust git TUI. https://github.com/extrawurst/gitui
- **k9s** — Kubernetes ops cockpit (good UX reference). https://github.com/derailed/k9s
- **lazydocker** — container cockpit. https://github.com/jesseduffield/lazydocker
Frameworks to build your own:
- **Textual** (Python). https://github.com/Textualize/textual
- **Bubble Tea** + **Bubbles/Lip Gloss** (Go). https://github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea
- **Ratatui** (Rust). https://github.com/ratatui/ratatui

## Suggested wiring
A pragmatic stack: **Backstage catalog** (or **Plane**) as the issue/entity graph → **Neo4j/GraphQL** query layer → **MCP** server exposing that graph as tools → agents orchestrated via **LangGraph**/**Agents SDK** speaking **A2A**/**Agent Protocol** → **gh-dash-style** cockpit built on **Textual**/**Bubble Tea** for the human view.

Note: I haven't verified these repos are live/maintained as of today — confirm current status and license before adopting.

# CRM / Practice Management Software for Dental Clinics (HIPAA-focused)

Dental clinics rarely use a generic "CRM" — they use **dental practice management systems (PMS)** that bundle CRM/patient-relationship features (recall, messaging, reviews) with clinical charting, imaging, and billing. HIPAA compliance for these vendors centers on a signed **Business Associate Agreement (BAA)**, encryption, audit logging, and access controls. Below are the main options, split by category.

> Verify each vendor's current HIPAA/BAA terms directly — compliance details change and I can't confirm live status.

## Full dental practice management (clinical + patient engagement)

- **Dentrix Ascend** — cloud-native sibling. https://www.dentrixascend.com/

## Patient-engagement / communication layer (the "CRM" part, sits on top of a PMS)

- **Weave** — phone + texting + reviews + payments; signs BAAs. https://www.getweave.com/
- **NexHealth** — scheduling, reminders, patient comms with a developer API. https://www.nexhealth.com/
- **Solutionreach** — recall, reminders, campaigns. https://www.solutionreach.com/

- **Podium** — reviews/messaging/payments, HIPAA options. https://www.podium.com/

## Generic HIPAA-compliant CRMs (if you truly want a sales/CRM tool, not a PMS)

- **Zoho CRM** — signs BAAs for HIPAA. https://www.zoho.com/crm/ (compliance: https://www.zoho.com/crm/hipaa-compliance.html)
- **HubSpot** — supports BAAs on higher tiers/with configuration. https://www.hubspot.com/ (see https://legal.hubspot.com/dpa for data terms)

## Niche / open-source (GitHub)

- **OpenEMR** — open-source EHR/practice management (general medical, adaptable, active HIPAA-hardening work). https://github.com/openemr/openemr — project site https://www.open-emr.org/

- **Incumbent / insurance-heavy workflows:** **Dentrix** or **Eaglesoft**.

## HIPAA checklist regardless of vendor
1. **Signed BAA** — non-negotiable; a vendor that won't sign one is disqualifying.
2. Encryption in transit and at rest.
3. Role-based access + audit logs.
4. Data-portability/export terms (avoid lock-in).
5. Breach-notification commitments.

Reference for BAA requirements: HHS — https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/covered-entities/sample-business-associate-agreement-provisions/index.html

results.prompt: Easy weeknight pasta recipe with mushrooms and spinach?
results.stdout:
# Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta (~25 min)

Fast, one-pan sauce, pantry-friendly. Serves 4.

## Ingredients
- 12 oz / 340 g pasta (penne, fettuccine, or spaghetti)
- 2 tbsp olive oil (or 1 tbsp oil + 1 tbsp butter)
- 8 oz / 225 g mushrooms, sliced (cremini or button)
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- 5 oz / 150 g fresh spinach
- ¾ cup / 180 ml cream (or half-and-half; or ½ cup pasta water + 2 tbsp cream cheese for lighter)
- ½ cup / 50 g grated Parmesan
- Salt, black pepper, pinch of chili flakes
- Optional: splash of white wine, squeeze of lemon

## Method
1. **Boil pasta** in well-salted water. Reserve ~1 cup pasta water before draining.
2. **Sear mushrooms**: heat oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add mushrooms in one layer, leave them undisturbed 2–3 min to brown, then stir and cook until golden (~5 min total). Season with salt.
3. **Aromatics**: lower heat to medium, add garlic (and wine if using); cook 30–60 sec until fragrant.
4. **Wilt spinach**: add spinach in handfuls, stirring until collapsed (~2 min).
5. **Sauce**: pour in cream, simmer 1–2 min, stir in Parmesan. Loosen with pasta water to desired consistency.
6. **Combine**: add drained pasta, toss to coat. Finish with pepper, chili flakes, and a squeeze of lemon. Taste for salt.

## Tips
- **Browning matters**: don't crowd the pan—mushrooms steam and turn gray if piled up. Work in batches if needed.
- **Protein add-ins**: white beans, grilled chicken, or crisped pancetta.
- **Vegan**: swap cream for full-fat coconut milk or a cashew cream, use nutritional yeast instead of Parmesan.
- **Extra savory**: a teaspoon of soy sauce or miso deepens the mushroom flavor.

Note: I skipped source citations here since the request was for a recipe, not tools or software projects — this is a standard technique-based dish rather than something attributable to a single primary URL.

results.prompt: Looking for open-source multi-agent frameworks for autonomous software development / AI SDLC. Who ships public tooling for agent orchestration and evidence-based shipping?
results.stdout:
The open-source landscape splits into two layers:

1. Agent orchestration: assigning, isolating, coordinating, and resuming work.
2. Evidence-based shipping: proving what ran, what changed, which tests passed, and why a result should merge.

Very few projects do both well. For a production AI SDLC, I’d compose an orchestrator with an evidence/evaluation layer rather than expect one framework to own the whole pipeline.

## Software-development-native orchestration

| Project | Best fit | Evidence posture |
|---|---|---|
| [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) | The strongest general-purpose open coding-agent platform: repo work, shell/browser tools, Docker execution, SDK, and GitHub workflows. | Good sandboxing and benchmark integration; not primarily a provenance ledger. See its [Software Agent SDK](https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/index). |
| [Gas Town](https://github.com/gastownhall/gastown) | Coordinating many Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Gemini, and other coding agents across persistent tasks. | Persistent work tracking, but you still need independent verification and CI gates. |
| [Overstory](https://github.com/jayminwest/overstory) | Niche, operator-oriented swarm orchestration with isolated workers, runtime adapters, and enforced role/tool boundaries. | Stronger execution controls than most small orchestrators; pair with CI and provenance capture. |
| [MetaGPT](https://github.com/FoundationAgents/MetaGPT) | Role-based “software company” workflows—product manager, architect, engineer, QA—with structured intermediate artifacts. | Useful artifact generation, but its agent-authored documents are not independent proof of correctness. |
| [ChatDev](https://github.com/OpenBMB/ChatDev) | Research and experimentation with role-playing software teams and evolving orchestration. | Conversation and generated artifacts are inspectable; production verification is not its center of gravity. |
| [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) | Reproducible repository-level issue resolution and coding-agent research. Mostly a coding-agent harness, not a broad multi-agent SDLC manager. | Excellent research evidence: JSON thought/action/observation trajectories, configs, logs, predictions, and SWE-bench integration are documented in its [trajectory format](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent/blob/main/docs/usage/trajectories.md). |

The newer niche projects—Gas Town and Overstory—are especially relevant if “multi-agent” means several real coding sessions working concurrently, rather than several personas exchanging messages inside one Python process.

## General orchestration frameworks

These are good foundations, but you must supply the Git/worktree, test, review, and release semantics:

- [Microsoft Agent Framework](https://github.com/microsoft/agent-framework) supports sequential, concurrent, handoff, and group collaboration workflows, plus checkpointing and human approval. It is Microsoft’s current successor to AutoGen.

- [AutoGen](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen) remains influential and includes AgentChat and AutoGen Bench, but it is now explicitly in maintenance mode. I would not start a new long-lived platform on it.

- [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) is the most flexible low-level choice for explicit state machines, durable execution, resumability, subgraphs, and human-in-the-loop gates. It is not software-development-specific.

- [CrewAI](https://github.com/crewAIInc/crewAI) offers an accessible split between autonomous “Crews” and deterministic event-driven “Flows.” Good for quickly expressing developer/reviewer/tester roles, but its role-play alone is not a quality system.

## Public tooling for evidence-based shipping

The most interesting projects here are less famous than the orchestrators:

- [h5i](https://github.com/h5i-dev/h5i) is the clearest direct match. It wraps agents in isolated Git workspaces and records prompts, model identity, commands, logs, policies, handoffs, reviews, verifier outcomes, and network activity in Git-backed provenance. Its [`h5i team`](https://h5i.dev/manual/) workflow adds sealed candidate workspaces, peer review, and one auditable merge. It is young, so evaluate maturity carefully.

- [SWE-bench](https://github.com/SWE-bench/SWE-bench) provides reproducible repository-level verification against real GitHub issues. It is a benchmark rather than a shipping system, but its model—patch plus isolated execution plus objective tests—is the right evidentiary pattern.

- [BenchFlow](https://github.com/benchflow-ai/benchflow) runs different coding agents against tasks in sandboxed environments. It is useful for regression-testing agent/model/prompt changes before promoting them into an SDLC.

- [PR-Agent](https://github.com/The-PR-Agent/pr-agent) is a community-maintained, self-hostable PR review layer. It can add review and improvement steps, but AI review findings should remain supplemental evidence, not merge authority.

- [AgentClash](https://github.com/AgentClash/agentclash) targets trajectory-level agent evaluation, including tool behavior, cost, latency, and recovery, with CI-oriented regression testing. It is more appropriate for testing your orchestration system than validating an individual application patch.

## My practical shortlist

For a production pilot, I would test one of these combinations:

- Maximum autonomy: Gas Town or Overstory → isolated Git worktrees → normal CI → h5i provenance → human merge.
- Framework-controlled pipeline: LangGraph or Microsoft Agent Framework → OpenHands/SWE-agent workers → deterministic test/security gates → PR-Agent as an advisory reviewer.
- Research and measurable improvement: SWE-agent/OpenHands → SWE-bench or BenchFlow → stored trajectories and patches → promote only configurations that improve held-out pass rates.
- Product-design-to-code experimentation: MetaGPT or ChatDev → hand generated artifacts to an actual coding worker → independently execute tests and acceptance checks.

The central rule is that agents must not certify their own work. A developer agent saying “tests pass,” followed by a reviewer agent agreeing, is still only model output. Strong evidence is independently captured command output, reproducible environments, exact commits and diffs, deterministic checks, security scans, evaluation trajectories, and an explicit human or policy-controlled merge gate.
