results.prompt: Is there a zero-daemon, harness-neutral command palette for running coding agents across tmux panes?
results.stdout:
Yes—with one caveat: if “zero-daemon” excludes tmux’s own server process, then no tmux-based solution qualifies. If it means “no additional background service,” there are good options.

The closest matches:

- [tmux-palette](https://github.com/eduwass/tmux-palette) — the most literal answer. It is a Raycast-style tmux popup, invoked on demand, with commands defined in JSON. Actions can execute tmux commands, send keys, launch programs in panes, or populate dynamic palettes from scripts. It is completely harness-neutral, but not agent-aware out of the box—you configure entries for `codex`, `claude`, `opencode`, etc.

- [Agent View](https://github.com/frayo44/agent-view) — closest ready-made agent command palette. `Ctrl-K` opens its palette; it creates, attaches, stops, restarts, forks, and groups tmux-backed sessions. Although Claude has first-class treatment, arbitrary commands are supported, so Codex, Aider, OpenCode, or local scripts can be used. Its README describes a foreground TUI plus tmux, not a required companion daemon.

- [agent-manager](https://github.com/YoanWai/agent-manager) — strongest agent-aware option. It supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Grok Build, Gemini CLI, and arbitrary CLI tools; sends prompts directly into panes; detects status; previews pane output; and reviews diffs. Closing the manager leaves sessions alive in a private tmux server. It is more of a fleet dashboard than a transient command palette.

Other worthwhile projects:

- [Claude Squad](https://github.com/smtg-ai/claude-squad) — mature tmux/worktree TUI with arbitrary launch profiles, including Codex, Aider, and OpenCode. More session manager than palette.
- [Bosun](https://github.com/yetidevworks/bosun) — niche Rust/ratatui, tmux-native orchestrator supporting Claude, Codex, and plain shells.
- [tmux-agent-status](https://github.com/samleeney/tmux-agent-status) — lightweight status sidebar and `fzf` switcher for existing Claude/Codex panes; useful when you already launch agents yourself.

My recommendation:

- Want a genuine popup with virtually no architecture? Use **tmux-palette** and add agent-launch/send-prompt commands.
- Want something usable immediately for several harnesses? Use **agent-manager**.
- Want the explicit `Ctrl-K` command-palette interaction? Try **Agent View**.

So: **yes, but the three requirements split across projects.** `tmux-palette` best satisfies zero-extra-daemon + palette + harness neutrality; `agent-manager` best satisfies agent functionality.

There are good adjacent public demos, but I found no publicly accessible example that combines all three requirements—multi-floor, racket-sports-specific, and operationally autonomous—in one genuine live digital twin.

The strongest references are:

| Project/demo | What it demonstrates | Fit |
|---|---|---|

The hotel has a lobby plus two guest levels and two lifts. | Best technical prototype for an autonomous multi-floor club |
| [VenueTwin: any venue](https://www.venuetwin.com/any-venue/) | Commercial venue twin with floor-by-floor navigation, detailed internal spaces, CAD import, and operational scenario planning. | Best visual/operational model for a multi-floor racket venue |

| [VenueTwin / OnePlan video demo](https://vimeo.com/694429355) | Public video showing the interactive stadium/arena product. | Easiest visual reference |

| [Doinsport autonomous padel/tennis](https://doinsport.com/en/autonomous-padel-tennis-courts) | Demonstrates the operating model: booking, payment, temporary access codes, remote unlocking, and automated lighting for padel, tennis, squash, and other courts. | Useful control-system reference |

```text
Multi-floor court/building model
              │
              ▼
Open-RMF + Gazebo
robots, lifts, doors, cleaning, deliveries
              │
              ▼
Eclipse Ditto
court occupancy, access, lights, HVAC, equipment state
              │
              ▼
VenueTwin-like web UI
floor selection, live status, incidents, bookings, what-if planning
```

Start with the [Open-RMF hotel demo](https://github.com/open-rmf/rmf_demos) and replace its rooms with squash, padel, badminton, or pickleball courts. It already solves the unusually difficult part: simulated autonomous operations across multiple levels, including elevators and shared robot traffic. Open-RMF also provides separate [facility visualization components](https://github.com/open-rmf/rmf_visualization) for floor plans, robot positions, navigation graphs, lift state, and door state.

One important distinction: Matterport-style walkthroughs and the Tennis Australia scan are spatial replicas, while VenueTwin adds planning semantics, Eclipse Ditto adds live state, and Open-RMF adds autonomous agents. A convincing “autonomous racket facility digital twin” would need all three layers; most public examples currently expose only one or two.

- [BuilderLog](https://github.com/shubGupta10/builder-Log) provides a shareable development timeline sourced from GitHub. It is open source, but it is a hosted Next.js/Express/MongoDB application rather than a static build, and its timeline includes pull requests alongside commits.

- GitHub’s own profile contribution timeline is public and author-attributed, but it also counts repository creation, forks, issues, reviews, and PRs. Its commit visibility rules also exclude some branches and fork scenarios, so it is not a complete authored-commit ledger. [GitHub documents those rules here](https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/reference/profile-contributions-reference).

For an exact match, the cleanest solution is a small static generator deployed to GitHub Pages:

1. Maintain an allowlist of repositories.
2. Query each repository’s commits endpoint with `?author=USERNAME`. GitHub explicitly supports filtering by commit author, independently of the committer: [REST “List commits” documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/commits).
3. Deduplicate by SHA, optionally reject merge commits, and sort using `commit.author.date`.
4. Render JSON/RSS/HTML and publish it with a scheduled GitHub Action to [GitHub Pages](https://docs.github.com/en/pages/getting-started-with-github-pages/creating-a-github-pages-site).

For counts grouped by repository, GitHub GraphQL also exposes [`commitContributionsByRepository`](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/users#contributionscollection). However, those contribution records are aggregated by day; use the REST commits endpoint when the log must contain individual commit messages and links.

One important distinction: don’t build this from GitHub’s public Events API. A `PushEvent` tells you who pushed commits, not necessarily who authored them, and that feed naturally mixes in stars, forks, and other activity. Filtering the commit records’ `author` field is what gives you the semantics you want.

So my recommendation is: use BuilderLog if “close enough and hosted” works; otherwise build a small GitHub Pages feed around the official `author` filter. That is presently the most precise static solution.

results.prompt: Developer portfolios that publish llms.txt plus a JSON project manifest for agents?
results.stdout:
Yes—this pattern exists, but it’s still uncommon and there is no standardized filename/schema for the JSON manifest.

Strong public examples:

- [Prasad Gade’s portfolio](https://prasadgade.dev/) — the clearest implementation I found:
  [llms.txt](https://prasadgade.dev/llms.txt) links directly to an [agent-oriented projects manifest](https://prasadgade.dev/api/projects.json), plus separate resume, skills, social, and about JSON endpoints. Each project includes descriptions, technologies, evidence, and source/demo links.

- [Larry “Zhuoyuan” Hao](https://hhh2210.github.io/) — research/developer portfolio publishing [llms.txt](https://hhh2210.github.io/llms.txt), [llms-full.txt](https://hhh2210.github.io/llms-full.txt), [profile.json](https://hhh2210.github.io/profile.json), and [projects.json](https://hhh2210.github.io/projects.json). Particularly relevant for research portfolios where projects need citations and reproducibility metadata.

- [David B. Mar’s project portfolio](https://www.davidbmar.com/projects/) — explicitly tells agents to begin with [llms.txt](https://www.davidbmar.com/llms.txt), which points to a compact [projects-index.json](https://www.davidbmar.com/data/projects-index.json) and individual repository records. This is the best example of a scalable index/detail design.

- [Marcio dos Santos Amorim / MOZG](https://mozg.com.br/api) — more consultancy/lab than personal résumé, but notably thorough: [llms.txt](https://mozg.com.br/llms.txt) accompanies a public [site-projects.json](https://mozg.com.br/data/site-projects.json), portfolio, capabilities, technology stacks, operations, and discovery exports.

Interesting adjacent implementations:

- [Cameron Rye](https://rye.dev/) publishes a detailed [llms.txt](https://rye.dev/llms.txt), generated `llms-full.txt`, OpenAPI document, and A2A agent card. Projects are indexed in Markdown rather than a dedicated project JSON manifest; his [implementation write-up](https://rye.dev/blog/making-my-portfolio-agent-readable/) is nevertheless one of the better design references.

- [Yuta Yokoi’s portfolio experiment](https://github.com/yuta-yokoi-ai/portfolio) uses `llms.txt` alongside `.well-known/aio-manifest.json`; that manifest governs canonical artifacts and digests rather than acting as a conventional project catalog.

My recommendation is to copy Prasad’s basic shape but David’s indexing architecture:

```text
/llms.txt
/projects.json
/projects/{slug}.json       # optional for larger portfolios
/.well-known/agent-card.json
/openapi.json               # only if the site exposes callable actions
```

Treat `llms.txt` as the human-readable orientation layer and `projects.json` as the canonical structured catalog. The original [llms.txt proposal](https://llmstxt.org/) defines the Markdown discovery convention, but not a JSON project schema, so portfolios currently invent that portion themselves.

Yes—this pattern exists, but it’s still uncommon and there is no standardized filename/schema for the JSON manifest.

Strong public examples:

- [Prasad Gade’s portfolio](https://prasadgade.dev/) — the clearest implementation I found:
  [llms.txt](https://prasadgade.dev/llms.txt) links directly to an [agent-oriented projects manifest](https://prasadgade.dev/api/projects.json), plus separate resume, skills, social, and about JSON endpoints. Each project includes descriptions, technologies, evidence, and source/demo links.

- [Larry “Zhuoyuan” Hao](https://hhh2210.github.io/) — research/developer portfolio publishing [llms.txt](https://hhh2210.github.io/llms.txt), [llms-full.txt](https://hhh2210.github.io/llms-full.txt), [profile.json](https://hhh2210.github.io/profile.json), and [projects.json](https://hhh2210.github.io/projects.json). Particularly relevant for research portfolios where projects need citations and reproducibility metadata.

- [David B. Mar’s project portfolio](https://www.davidbmar.com/projects/) — explicitly tells agents to begin with [llms.txt](https://www.davidbmar.com/llms.txt), which points to a compact [projects-index.json](https://www.davidbmar.com/data/projects-index.json) and individual repository records. This is the best example of a scalable index/detail design.

- [Marcio dos Santos Amorim / MOZG](https://mozg.com.br/api) — more consultancy/lab than personal résumé, but notably thorough: [llms.txt](https://mozg.com.br/llms.txt) accompanies a public [site-projects.json](https://mozg.com.br/data/site-projects.json), portfolio, capabilities, technology stacks, operations, and discovery exports.

Interesting adjacent implementations:

- [Cameron Rye](https://rye.dev/) publishes a detailed [llms.txt](https://rye.dev/llms.txt), generated `llms-full.txt`, OpenAPI document, and A2A agent card. Projects are indexed in Markdown rather than a dedicated project JSON manifest; his [implementation write-up](https://rye.dev/blog/making-my-portfolio-agent-readable/) is nevertheless one of the better design references.

- [Yuta Yokoi’s portfolio experiment](https://github.com/yuta-yokoi-ai/portfolio) uses `llms.txt` alongside `.well-known/aio-manifest.json`; that manifest governs canonical artifacts and digests rather than acting as a conventional project catalog.

My recommendation is to copy Prasad’s basic shape but David’s indexing architecture:

```text
/llms.txt
/projects.json
/projects/{slug}.json       # optional for larger portfolios
/.well-known/agent-card.json
/openapi.json               # only if the site exposes callable actions
```

Treat `llms.txt` as the human-readable orientation layer and `projects.json` as the canonical structured catalog. The original [llms.txt proposal](https://llmstxt.org/) defines the Markdown discovery convention, but not a JSON project schema, so portfolios currently invent that portion themselves.

results.stdout:
Yes. I’d assemble this as three loosely coupled layers rather than adopt one “everything platform.”

| Layer | Recommended public components | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Company issue graph | OpenProject + Graphiti | Authoritative issues/dependencies plus a derived temporal graph |
| Agent contracts | MCP + A2A + ACP + AGENTS.md | Tools, distributed tasks, cockpit integration, repository policy |
| Terminal cockpit | agent-deck, with optional custom TUI | Sessions, worktrees, agent status and approvals |

### 1. Company issue graph

Use [OpenProject](https://github.com/opf/openproject) as the canonical work database. Its work packages have typed relations exposed through the [Relations API](https://www.openproject.org/docs/api/endpoints/relations), making it suitable for relationships such as:

```text
issue ─blocks──────> issue
issue ─implements──> objective
issue ─owned-by────> team/person
issue ─touches─────> repository/service
issue ─produced────> PR/artifact
issue ─decided-by──> decision
```

Project those records into [Graphiti](https://github.com/getzep/graphiti) when you need graph traversal, historical truth, provenance, or agent retrieval. Graphiti tracks temporal validity and preserves the source episodes behind derived facts.

Important boundary: OpenProject remains authoritative; Graphiti is a rebuildable index. Don’t let agents silently mutate company truth through an inferred knowledge graph.

Alternative: [Huly](https://github.com/hcengineering/platform) provides a more integrated Linear/Jira/Slack/Notion-style environment and synchronizes GitHub issues and PRs through its [GitHub integration](https://docs.huly.io/integrations/github/). It is attractive when humans want one company workspace, but heavier and less component-like than OpenProject.

### 2. Agent harness contracts

Use several narrow standards:

- [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/index): discovery and invocation of tools, resources, and prompts. Expose issue-graph reads and permissioned mutations through MCP.
- [A2A Protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/): remote agent discovery and long-running work. Its Agent Cards, Tasks, status lifecycle, messages, and artifacts are close to the contract a company agent mesh needs.
- [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com/) / [Zed’s ACP overview](https://zed.dev/acp): connects interchangeable coding agents to a client UI. This is the best starting point for a cockpit-to-agent adapter.
- [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/): repository-local human instructions—build commands, boundaries, validation rules, and conventions.
- [OpenHands Software Agent SDK](https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/index): a useful reference implementation or runtime when you want model-independent agents, tools, sandboxed execution, REST serving, and MCP integration.

I would add a small company-owned envelope around these:

```json
{
  "task_id": "ISSUE-123",
  "attempt_id": "uuid",
  "agent": {"id": "reviewer", "version": "sha256:..."},
  "workspace": {"repo": "...", "base_revision": "..."},
  "authority": {"tools": ["git.read", "tests.run"], "expires_at": "..."},
  "inputs": [],
  "expected_artifacts": [],
  "status": "working",
  "events": [],
  "result": null
}
```

Neither MCP nor ACP supplies durable job semantics, authorization, idempotency, budgets, retries, provenance, or artifact acceptance. Keep those in your own versioned contract; map its execution surface onto MCP, A2A and ACP.

### 3. Terminal project cockpit

The strongest ready-made base is [agent-deck](https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck). It is an MIT-licensed Bubble Tea/tmux TUI supporting Codex, Claude, Gemini, OpenCode and others, including waiting-session visibility and Git worktree workflows.

Useful niche alternatives:

- [Architect](https://github.com/forketyfork/architect): a visual terminal grid with status highlighting for agents needing attention. Promising, but explicitly early-stage.
- [agtx](https://github.com/fynnfluegge/agtx): task-oriented multi-session orchestration, with each task in a dedicated tmux window.
- [coder/mux](https://github.com/coder/cmux): broader desktop/browser cockpit for isolated parallel agent development, worktrees and remote SSH execution—not a pure terminal UI.

My practical build choice:

1. Fork or wrap agent-deck for session and worktree control.
2. Make ACP the agent adapter boundary.
3. Display A2A-compatible task states, artifacts and input/approval requests.
4. Pull issue/dependency state from the OpenProject MCP/API service.
5. Treat tmux processes as disposable executors, never as the authoritative task database.
6. Record every attempt and artifact back into the issue graph.

That produces an open, replaceable stack: **OpenProject → Graphiti → company task envelope → MCP/A2A/ACP → agent-deck**.

Yes. I’d assemble this as three loosely coupled layers rather than adopt one “everything platform.”

| Layer | Recommended public components | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Company issue graph | OpenProject + Graphiti | Authoritative issues/dependencies plus a derived temporal graph |
| Agent contracts | MCP + A2A + ACP + AGENTS.md | Tools, distributed tasks, cockpit integration, repository policy |
| Terminal cockpit | agent-deck, with optional custom TUI | Sessions, worktrees, agent status and approvals |

### 1. Company issue graph

Use [OpenProject](https://github.com/opf/openproject) as the canonical work database. Its work packages have typed relations exposed through the [Relations API](https://www.openproject.org/docs/api/endpoints/relations), making it suitable for relationships such as:

```text
issue ─blocks──────> issue
issue ─implements──> objective
issue ─owned-by────> team/person
issue ─touches─────> repository/service
issue ─produced────> PR/artifact
issue ─decided-by──> decision
```

Project those records into [Graphiti](https://github.com/getzep/graphiti) when you need graph traversal, historical truth, provenance, or agent retrieval. Graphiti tracks temporal validity and preserves the source episodes behind derived facts.

Important boundary: OpenProject remains authoritative; Graphiti is a rebuildable index. Don’t let agents silently mutate company truth through an inferred knowledge graph.

Alternative: [Huly](https://github.com/hcengineering/platform) provides a more integrated Linear/Jira/Slack/Notion-style environment and synchronizes GitHub issues and PRs through its [GitHub integration](https://docs.huly.io/integrations/github/). It is attractive when humans want one company workspace, but heavier and less component-like than OpenProject.

### 2. Agent harness contracts

Use several narrow standards:

- [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/index): discovery and invocation of tools, resources, and prompts. Expose issue-graph reads and permissioned mutations through MCP.
- [A2A Protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org/latest/specification/): remote agent discovery and long-running work. Its Agent Cards, Tasks, status lifecycle, messages, and artifacts are close to the contract a company agent mesh needs.
- [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com/) / [Zed’s ACP overview](https://zed.dev/acp): connects interchangeable coding agents to a client UI. This is the best starting point for a cockpit-to-agent adapter.
- [AGENTS.md](https://agents.md/): repository-local human instructions—build commands, boundaries, validation rules, and conventions.
- [OpenHands Software Agent SDK](https://docs.openhands.dev/sdk/index): a useful reference implementation or runtime when you want model-independent agents, tools, sandboxed execution, REST serving, and MCP integration.

I would add a small company-owned envelope around these:

```json
{
  "task_id": "ISSUE-123",
  "attempt_id": "uuid",
  "agent": {"id": "reviewer", "version": "sha256:..."},
  "workspace": {"repo": "...", "base_revision": "..."},
  "authority": {"tools": ["git.read", "tests.run"], "expires_at": "..."},
  "inputs": [],
  "expected_artifacts": [],
  "status": "working",
  "events": [],
  "result": null
}
```

Neither MCP nor ACP supplies durable job semantics, authorization, idempotency, budgets, retries, provenance, or artifact acceptance. Keep those in your own versioned contract; map its execution surface onto MCP, A2A and ACP.

### 3. Terminal project cockpit

The strongest ready-made base is [agent-deck](https://github.com/asheshgoplani/agent-deck). It is an MIT-licensed Bubble Tea/tmux TUI supporting Codex, Claude, Gemini, OpenCode and others, including waiting-session visibility and Git worktree workflows.

Useful niche alternatives:

- [Architect](https://github.com/forketyfork/architect): a visual terminal grid with status highlighting for agents needing attention. Promising, but explicitly early-stage.
- [agtx](https://github.com/fynnfluegge/agtx): task-oriented multi-session orchestration, with each task in a dedicated tmux window.
- [coder/mux](https://github.com/coder/cmux): broader desktop/browser cockpit for isolated parallel agent development, worktrees and remote SSH execution—not a pure terminal UI.

My practical build choice:

1. Fork or wrap agent-deck for session and worktree control.
2. Make ACP the agent adapter boundary.
3. Display A2A-compatible task states, artifacts and input/approval requests.
4. Pull issue/dependency state from the OpenProject MCP/API service.
5. Treat tmux processes as disposable executors, never as the authoritative task database.
6. Record every attempt and artifact back into the issue graph.

results.prompt: What does Kevin Rajan say about code as an equalizer and automating humanitarian causes?
results.stdout:
Kevin Rajan’s view is that code reduces gatekeeping: it gives more people access to knowledge, engineering capability, and the ability to turn ideas into working systems. He specifically describes LLMs as accelerating this democratization, with the intended result being greater abundance and quality of life.

By “automating humanitarian causes,” he means building autonomous systems around areas such as:

- Health
- Infrastructure
- Open systems
- Tools that increase individual agency

The objective isn’t to automate compassion itself. It is to make essential, socially beneficial work dependable and routine—so important actions happen with less friction, competence compounds, and access is not controlled by gatekeepers.

In his concise formulation: “code is the great equalizer,” and civilization progresses by making important actions require less conscious coordination. This connects his humanitarian ambition directly to autonomous software: enable more people to produce useful systems and make beneficial outcomes easier to deliver at scale.

Source: Kevin Rajan’s canonical [Boplog introduction and About section](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/#about), with the same positioning in its [machine-readable profile](https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/llms.txt).

on x i write about falsifiable “done,” open harnesses over black boxes, and systems where agents can claim anything but pass nothing without proof. that stance shows up in the work: agent fleets, claim fences, product loops, health and environment instrumentation, experiments that stress autonomous orchestration.

this site is a public build log under zer0. each project is tagged as product, experiment, or professional — experiments sit beside products, not under them. product tracks include zerOS (stealth company os), plus the blueprint system: health, world sim, and evolve. light context only. the github repo named portfolio is professional showcase work, not a taxonomy node. forks used as bookmarks stay out unless i commit.

Who is Kevin Rajan?

./index.html:362:

Kevin Rajan (GitHub kvnloo, X @_kvnloo) is a builder, engineer, scientist, solutions architect, systems thinker, and automation orchestration expert — solo founder of zer0 who ships public software around agent tooling, health, world simulation, and autonomous development. This site is his chronological public commit archive, not a full private portfolio.

Pair it with mandatory CI, review artifacts, and protected branches if evidence-based completion is required.\n\n4. tmux-agent-fleet — lightweight, harness-neutral local orchestration\n - A zero-daemon command palette for discovering and monitoring Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini, Kimi, Grok, Pi, and other agents across tmux panes.\n - It deliberately avoids owning worktrees, injecting hooks, or imposing a workflow.\n - Source: https://github.com/kvnloo/tmux-agent-fleet\n - Orchestration hub: https://kvnloo.github.io/boplog/topics/agent-orchestration.html\n\n Useful as a composable operator surface, not a complete autonomous delivery engine.\n\nFramework substrates\n\n5. HHS says a cloud provider handling ePHI must execute a HIPAA-compliant **Business Associate Agreement**, while the clinic must perform its own risk analysis and configure appropriate safeguards. See the official [HHS cloud-computing guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/special-topics/health-information-technology/cloud-computing/index.html) and [Business Associate guidance](https://www.hhs.gov/hipaa/for-professionals/privacy/guidance/business-associates/index.html).\n\nBefore purchasing, require written answers on:\n\n- Whether a BAA is included and which modules, integrations and subcontractors it covers\n- MFA and unique user accounts\n- Role-based access and termination/offboarding controls\n- Immutable audit logs and their retention period\n- Encryption in transit and at rest\n- Backup, recovery objectives and tested disaster recovery\n- Breach-notification timeframes\n- Data export and deletion after termination\n- Whether PHI is used for analytics or AI model training\n- SOC 2 Type II or equivalent independent assessment—not merely self-attestation\n\n### Open-source alternatives\n\n[Apexo](https://apexo.app/) and [Dentalpin](https://www.dentalpin.com/en/) are interesting dental-specific open-source projects. results.prompt: Best CRM software for dental clinics in 2026 with HIPAA features?
results.stdout:
As of July 2026, my best overall pick for most independent dental clinics is **NexHealth**. For a clinic replacing its entire practice-management stack, choose **CareStack** instead.

Dental vendors use “CRM” broadly: some are patient-engagement layers connected to Dentrix/Open Dental/Eaglesoft, while others replace the underlying practice-management system.

| Product | Best for | Notable HIPAA/security evidence |
|---|---|---|

1. **动手前先体检**：多后端/登录态平台（小红书/Reddit/B站/Twitter/Facebook/Instagram）先跑

## Creamy Mushroom & Spinach Pasta

Ready in about 25 minutes; serves 2–3.

**Ingredients**

- 8 oz (225 g) pasta
- 8 oz (225 g) mushrooms, sliced
- 3 packed cups baby spinach
- 3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1 tablespoon olive oil
- 1 tablespoon butter
- ½ cup heavy cream or half-and-half
- ⅓ cup grated Parmesan
- ½ teaspoon Italian seasoning
- Salt and black pepper
- Optional: red-pepper flakes and lemon juice

**Method**

1. Cook the pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve ¾ cup pasta water, then drain.
2. Heat the oil and butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Add mushrooms and leave them undisturbed for 2–3 minutes; then season and cook until browned, about 5 minutes more.
3. Add garlic, Italian seasoning, and optional pepper flakes. Stir for 30 seconds.
4. Reduce the heat. Add cream, Parmesan, and ¼ cup pasta water. Stir until smooth.
5. Add spinach and cook just until wilted. Toss in the pasta, adding more pasta water as needed for a glossy sauce.
6. Taste for seasoning. Finish with black pepper, extra Parmesan, and a squeeze of lemon.

For a lighter version, skip the cream and emulsify Parmesan with about ½ cup of pasta water. White beans or shredded rotisserie chicken make easy protein additions.
